---
title: "The Joint Effects of Measurement Error and Model Misspecification on Statistical Interactions"
---
**Presenter:** Aljoscha Rimpler, University of Groningen

**Co-authors:** Henk Kiers (University of Groningen), Don van Ravenzwaaij (University of Groningen)

### Abstract {.unlisted .unnumbered}

Interaction effects are frequently hypothesized but often fail to replicate in psychology. Typically, what researchers would like to investigate is the effect of a predictor on an outcome, conditional on another predictor variable. These interaction effects are modeled as product terms in psychological research. However, these effects are oftentimes difficult to replicate, they often make the model unstable and they lead to overfitting — particularly when observed measures are noisy. A natural response is to omit interaction effects when they appear unreliable. But what are the consequences of omitting a true interaction effect under noisy measurement conditions?

It is commonly assumed that measurement error simply attenuates effects toward zero. We show this assumption fails when true interaction effects exist. Using closed form analytical derivations, we demonstrate that measurement error and the omission of interaction effects are entangled in the regression, producing a joint bias which cannot be decomposed into its components and thus cannot be corrected separately. The consequences are counterintuitive: a model omitting an interaction can simultaneously be more biased and more stable across repetitions than the correctly specified one. This can be accompanied by fit metrics so similar that even for infinite samples, the models are barely distinguishable.
